title: The Future of Generative AI in the Court System & The Importance of Transparency — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The excerpt introduces judicial opinion drafting as a topic and describes the hosts’ general experiences with generative AI positively, but it provides no developed recommendation that lawyers or judges should actively shape deployment, no implementation or governance proposal, and no substantive discussion of responsible experimentation.
qs: Today's episode is our second in a two-part series on courts and generative AI, so we'll talk specifically about judicial use of generative AI for drafting opinions.

Our first is what we call our Gen AI Moments, which are the times since our last recording when each of us has used generative AI and found it to be really stunning, almost magical, and very helpful in our day-to-day work.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts cautious, bounded court adoption and materially develops the cluster with specific court-side evidence on public-funding and training constraints, record-linked operational tools, exploratory judicial reasoning, and transitional transparency to sustain public confidence. Its capability claims remain examples and predictions rather than proof of improved justice outcomes.
qs: I've said before that I think courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.
Whether it’s required by appellate courts or not, I think it’s going to be valuable to building public confidence in what we do.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts exploratory AI use before technological certainty and materially develops the cluster’s practitioner-engagement proposition for courts. It identifies public-resource and training constraints as implementation barriers while arguing that operational experimentation can coexist with preserving litigants’ voices; however, it offers no effectiveness evidence.
qs: I've said before that I think courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.
There's plenty of room to hear a litigant's voice and also improve your operations.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts selective augmentation by treating operational improvement as compatible with preserving litigants’ human voices. It materially extends the cluster’s implementation argument by identifying public funding, tool scarcity and inadequate training as court-specific constraints that may widen the public–private adoption gap.
qs: There's plenty of room to hear a litigant's voice and also improve your operations.
I've said before that I think courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s organisational-change framing and materially extends it to courts: adoption depends on public funding, training and AI literacy, while service redesign must preserve litigants’ voices and provide transitional transparency about consequential uses.
qs: I've said before that I think courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.

But I think along the way, and especially for institutions like courts, or even in alternative dispute resolution, the more transparent we can be with the people we serve about how we’re using the technology is going to be valuable.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that effective legal-AI use depends on institutional capacity, training and context rather than mere tool availability, and materially extends the synthesis to courts by identifying public-sector resource constraints and proposing transitional, context-sensitive transparency for judicial use. It does not independently establish jagged task capability or verification performance.
qs: It's just very, very hard for courts to keep up with this technology given how quickly it's moving and how hard it is to figure out how to use it well.

But I think along the way, and especially for institutions like courts, or even in alternative dispute resolution, the more transparent we can be with the people we serve about how we’re using the technology is going to be valuable.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source is consistent with the cluster’s distinction between AI assistance and machine adjudication: it presents the Frances Kellor bot as an exploratory tool for considering future dispute-resolution initiatives and community engagement, not as an adjudicator or source of authoritative legal decisions. It offers no performance evidence and does not materially develop the cluster’s broader claims about access, safeguards or legitimacy.
qs: Now we can ask this bot questions about some of the things we're thinking about doing in the future.
I think it'll be a fun tool for our community to play with.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI adoption alone cannot produce meaningful access gains. McCormack sees operational improvement as compatible with preserving litigants’ voices, but makes successful court deployment conditional on adequate public funding, training and institutional resources; Leonard likewise warns that courts may lag better-resourced private actors.
qs: I've said before that I think courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.
I feel like that particular concern can be addressed—if the resource issue can be solved.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI value depends on institutional readiness rather than access alone. It identifies courts’ public-funding constraints, limited access to tools and insufficient training resources as structural barriers to effective adoption, while treating operational improvement as conditional on resolving those constraints.
qs: I've said before that I think courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.
So I feel like courts are at a real disadvantage in trying to keep up and give their teams the resources to learn how to use these tools.

kp.k: Survey suggests judicial caution and uncertainty about appropriate uses
kp.d: Leonard reports that a recent Thomson Reuters survey found neutrality to be the primary sentiment toward generative AI among judges and court administrators, with concern second, whereas law firm lawyers' second reaction was optimism. She reports concerns about losing litigants' first-person accounts through computer-generated language and uncertainty about appropriate court uses. The transcript provides neither sample size nor survey methodology.
qs: the primary sentiment was neutrality—a sort of "wait and see" approach to whether generative AI is actually helpful, useful, and ethical to use.
court administrators and judges were more likely to report that their second reaction was concern.
people just aren't sure how they should be using generative AI tools in the work they do for the courts.

kp.k: Public funding constrains court training and technology adoption
kp.d: McCormack cites 18% of courts reporting any training and attributes judicial concern partly to resource disadvantages arising from politically determined public funding, expensive tools and rapid technological change. Both speakers worry that private-sector adoption will outpace courts. McCormack argues that preserving litigants' voices is compatible with operational improvements, conditional on solving resource constraints.
qs: I'm surprised that 18% of courts report having any training.
courts are at such a disadvantage because they rely on public funding—and public funding is a political process for all of their resources.
There's plenty of room to hear a litigant's voice and also improve your operations.
our shared concern that the private sector will move with these tools much faster than public institutions will—courts especially.

kp.k: Record-linked AI could streamline adversarial litigation
kp.d: McCormack describes Clearbrief as a legal-AI product that assembles facts and links them to their sources in the record, with potential shared use across disputing parties. She reports benefits at a few adopting courts, without quantitative evidence, and suggests that identifying agreed and disputed facts could reduce wasted effort. She predicts greater judicial comfort as operationally useful products become more visible.
qs: What it does is pull together all of the facts and then show you where each fact comes from in the record.
If you're willing, you can even share it among all of the parties in a dispute.
If we could all agree up front on which facts are not in dispute and which ones are, it would save so much time and energy—so we could focus only on the points where people are going to disagree.
I predict we'll see a growing comfort level with the technology.

kp.k: Newsom's concurrence illustrates AI-assisted ordinary-meaning interpretation
kp.d: Leonard recounts Judge Kevin Newsom's use of ChatGPT to consider whether an in-ground trampoline constituted landscaping in an insurance dispute after dictionary research proved unhelpful. She says he disclosed prompts and responses in a concurrence and later specifies that this use did not affect the ultimate holding. Her account of other judges' reactions, reported through outlets including Law.com, ranges from approval to concerns about training-data bias, limitations and hallucinations.
qs: He actually asked ChatGPT, "Could an in-ground trampoline be considered landscaping?"
He was very transparent about his use of ChatGPT and even shared his prompts and the AI's responses in his concurrence.
partly because of the biased data underlying their training, and partly because of the limitations and the hallucinations that LLMs can produce.
It didn’t impact the ultimate holding, but as you said, was an invitation to think about how LLMs could be used.

kp.k: Corpus linguistics supplies an analogy for judicial AI use
kp.d: McCormack links LLM-assisted interpretation to earlier judicial use of corpus linguistics, citing Michigan, Utah and Justice Breyer. She argues that broader collections of ordinary language can assist interpretation where conventional tools are imperfect, while distinguishing transparent, knowable corpora from undisclosed LLM training data and different analytical technologies. Her recommendation is supplementary, transparent use, not a claim that LLM interpretation is established as reliable.
qs: In a way, I feel like corpus linguistics in judicial decision-making was the precursor to ChatGPT in judicial decision-making.
The texts that are in corpora are knowable, so it's totally transparent. We don't know all the training data in LLMs.
So I think I'm similarly persuaded that this technology is at least another tool that judges could—and in some cases probably should—use.
Transparently again, telling their readers and colleagues what they used and what their prompts were, to help understand terms that are not perfectly clear.

kp.k: Reported Claude experiment suggests appellate drafting capabilities
kp.d: McCormack reports Adam Unikowsky's experiment feeding Claude Opus all merits briefs from all cases argued in the U.S. Supreme Court 'this term' and requesting three-paragraph decisions. She says almost every result matched the Court's disposition and that Unikowsky found some divergent opinions more persuasive. She attributes to him the assessment that Claude could perform elite appellate clerk work and perhaps a justice's work. These are reported experimental results and subjective assessments; no case count or detailed evaluation protocol is provided, and she acknowledges continuing model problems.
qs: he fed all of the merits briefs from all of the cases argued in the U.S. Supreme Court this term into Claude Opus.
And he asked Claude to write a three-paragraph opinion deciding each case. And in almost every case, it wrote an opinion consistent with the way the U.S. Supreme Court decided the case.
In a few cases where it didn’t write an opinion consistent with the U.S. Supreme Court, Adam himself was persuaded by Claude’s opinion more so than the U.S. Supreme Court’s opinion
Claude is absolutely capable of doing the work of, you know, the fanciest appellate law clerks we have right now, and maybe even a justice.
that’s not saying that it doesn’t still have some of the problems we’ve talked about many times in the course of this podcast.

kp.k: AI may generate solutions beyond parties' proposed legal arguments
kp.d: McCormack says Unikowsky also asked Claude to devise a new legal test neither party had suggested. Drawing on this example and her account of LLM-assisted idea generation at the AAA, she anticipates expanded uses for judges, arbitrators and mediators developing creative resolutions. Leonard likewise sees potential for trial and appellate litigators, supported by her personal experience obtaining unfamiliar perspectives from AI rather than measured legal outcomes.
qs: Will you come up with another way, a new test that neither party suggested, for how we could decide this hard legal question?
We do a lot of idea generation at the AAA around hard questions and hard problems, but now we always have the help of our LLM friends.
I could see litigators at trial and appellate courts, and judges, using it in just the way that Adam’s suggesting.
I really do think there’s an exciting future for this technology in resolving disputes.

kp.k: Blanket judicial disclosure requirements remain contested
kp.d: Leonard reports a conference discussion in which one view favored disclosure so appellate courts could distinguish human-generated from AI-generated content. McCormack accepts the importance of appellate courts knowing the information available below but questions whether this entails disclosing every technological contribution. She analogizes AI assistance to undisclosed clerk contributions, prior judicial research and research platforms. Both speculate that routine integration could make current disclosure debates appear naive five or ten years later.
qs: One perspective being that you would have to disclose usage so that appellate courts would know when the human judge created content and when a Gen AI created content.
But I’m not sure that it makes sense that disclosing your use of the technology in the course of your decision-making as a trial judge really follows from that.
trial judges don’t record what work exactly their law clerks did to help them with coming up with a particular decision in the case.
They don’t disclose Westlaw or other legal research tools—which more and more have this technology built into them.
five years, ten years from now, we should replay this conversation and it’ll seem a little naive at the front end of all of it.

kp.k: Transitional transparency supports confidence, alongside judicial AI literacy
kp.d: Despite questioning blanket disclosure obligations, McCormack favors maximum feasible transparency during the transition, particularly for courts and alternative dispute resolution, to build public confidence irrespective of appellate requirements. Leonard distinguishes consequential interpretive uses from routine drafting assistance and envisages clerks incorporating AI-workshopped language without judges knowing its origin, while judges still review and edit. She stresses literacy, training and discussion as necessary to navigate these developments.
qs: If it’s something that the case will hinge on and you want to know where the definition came from or where the concept came from.
I can imagine appellate law clerks drafting opinions and workshopping the language and then plugging it into the opinion without the judge even knowing
But all of that requires a lot of literacy and training and conversation.
my instinct is in favor of as much transparency as possible in this liminal period we’re in.
Whether it’s required by appellate courts or not, I think it’s going to be valuable to building public confidence in what we do.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Public courts risk falling behind private-sector AI adoption, but operational improvements need not erase litigants' voices.
pts.d: Bridget McCormack attributes courts' adoption disadvantage to dependence on politically allocated public funding and scarce, expensive tools. She considers the concern about losing litigants' voices addressable if resource constraints can be solved. Jen Leonard shares the expectation that private institutions will adopt faster.

pts.k: Record-focused legal AI can improve court operations and make litigation more efficient; visible benefits should increase adoption comfort.
pts.d: McCormack identifies Clearbrief's ability to assemble facts and show their sources in the record as an existing capability. She predicts that shared factual grounding could reduce unnecessary adversarial work and that more visibly useful products will increase courts' comfort with AI. These efficiency expectations are qualitative, not quantified findings.

pts.k: LLMs could supplement judges' tools for interpreting ordinary meaning.
pts.d: McCormack endorses transparent use of LLMs as an additional interpretive aid, drawing on the discussion of Judge Kevin Newsom's concurrence and her experience with corpus linguistics. She does not present this as autonomous judicial decision-making or as proof that AI interpretation is superior. Leonard notes that Newsom's use in the concurrence did not affect the ultimate holding.

pts.k: AI can help develop persuasive positions and novel solutions to legal disputes.
pts.d: McCormack predicts expanding uses in courts, arbitration and mediation, particularly generating solutions neither party has proposed. Leonard describes persuasive ability as already deployable and anticipates use by litigators and judges. McCormack reports an experiment by Adam Unikowsky as supporting context; his stronger comparison between Claude and elite appellate clerks or a justice is a secondhand assessment, not an independently demonstrated finding of the episode.

pts.k: Routine AI integration may make blanket disclosure expectations seem outdated, while transitional transparency can build public confidence.
pts.d: Leonard speculates that AI will become sufficiently embedded in ordinary work that today's broad disclosure debate may later seem dated. McCormack agrees, distinguishing a preference for transparency during the transition from a claim that appellate courts must require disclosure of every use. Leonard separately identifies disclosure as relevant when the case hinges on an AI-derived definition or concept.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: A reported survey supports the discussion of current judicial attitudes and limited training, rather than demonstrating future adoption outcomes.
pts.d: Leonard summarizes a recent Thomson Reuters survey of judges and court administrators: neutrality was the primary sentiment and concern the second, unlike law-firm lawyers' optimism. McCormack cites 18% of courts reporting any training. The transcript gives no sample size, field dates or methodological detail. McCormack's explanation linking concern to resources is her interpretation, informed by her court leadership experience.

pts.k: Operational and interpretive claims rely on reported early uses and a judicial example.
pts.d: McCormack cites qualitative reports of benefits in a few Clearbrief-using courts, without operational metrics. Leonard recounts Newsom's use of ChatGPT to consider whether an in-ground trampoline could count as landscaping, including publication of prompts and responses. McCormack also draws an analogy to courts' earlier use of corpus linguistics, while acknowledging differences in transparency and technology.

pts.k: Claims about legal reasoning and creativity draw on a secondhand experiment and personal experience.
pts.d: McCormack reports that Unikowsky supplied Claude Opus with merits briefs for all cases argued in the then-current U.S. Supreme Court term and requested three-paragraph decisions. She says almost all agreed with the Court's outcomes and describes a further request for a new legal test. No numerical success rate, experimental controls or independent evaluation is supplied. Her AAA ideation experience and Leonard's experience developing interpersonal positions provide additional anecdotal support, not measured legal performance.

pts.k: Disclosure predictions rest on analogy and expectations of embedded AI, not outcome data.
pts.d: McCormack compares AI assistance with existing undisclosed contributions from clerks, prior research and legal research tools. Her prediction that transparency builds public confidence is expressed as an institutional judgment; the episode provides no empirical test of that effect.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The episode distinguishes present capabilities from conditional adoption forecasts and a five-to-ten-year normalization horizon.
pts.d: In the 2024 episode, Clearbrief use, Newsom's concurrence and the Claude experiment are presented as existing or recent examples. More widespread court comfort depends on accessible products demonstrating benefits and on resources for training. Shared-record efficiencies depend on parties' willingness to share and identify factual agreement. McCormack's five-to-ten-year remark concerns how the disclosure conversation may appear retrospectively, not a firm deadline for universal adoption.

pts.k: Judicial use is qualified by transparency, training and unresolved model limitations.
pts.d: McCormack's interpretive endorsement calls for explaining the tools and prompts used. She distinguishes knowable corpus-linguistics texts from opaque LLM training data and retains reservations about model problems. Leonard reports other judges' concerns about bias and hallucinations and emphasizes literacy and training. These qualifications accompany augmentation claims; the speakers do not establish safe unsupervised adjudication.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Courts, judges, clerks and litigators face changed operations, research and drafting workflows.
pts.d: Courts and their teams face resource and learning disadvantages relative to private institutions. Judges could gain interpretive and idea-generation assistance; litigators could use record tools and develop new positions. Leonard imagines appellate clerks incorporating AI-assisted language into opinions without judges necessarily knowing its provenance, with judges continuing to review and edit the writing. No staffing reduction or employment forecast is made.

pts.k: Disputing parties, arbitrators, mediators and the public could benefit from more focused disputes, creative solutions and transparent institutional use.
pts.d: McCormack anticipates time and effort savings when parties agree on which facts are contested, and broader problem-solving opportunities for courts and alternative dispute resolution. The anticipated beneficiaries include individuals, organizations and businesses in disputes. Her public-confidence claim concerns transparency toward people served by courts and ADR institutions; the episode does not quantify savings or claim a measured reduction in unmet civil legal need.
